Series::beta¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::beta(double other) const

What It Does¶

beta() computes the beta function B(a, b) elementwise. self supplies a; the argument supplies b:

B(a, b) = Gamma(a) * Gamma(b) / Gamma(a + b)

The beta function is the normalizing constant of the Beta distribution and the value of the Euler integral integral_0^1 t^(a-1) (1 - t)^(b-1) dt. It appears in the Beta and Dirichlet densities, in the binomial coefficient (1 / ((n + 1) B(n - k + 1, k + 1))), and in the t and F distribution normalizers.

Use betaln() when the normalizer belongs in a logarithmic calculation; beta() can underflow even while the logarithm remains finite.

Properties:

  • Symmetric: B(a, b) = B(b, a).

  • B(1, 1) = 1; B(a, 1) = 1/a.

  • B(a, b) > 0 for a, b > 0; poles of the gamma factors at non-positive integer arguments propagate through.

Parameters¶

other (double): the second shape parameter b, a constant broadcast against every element of self.

Returns¶

Series beta() returns B(a, b) with the same shape as self. An integral input is promoted to float64.

Gradient¶

beta() is differentiable with respect to a (self). Its derivative is:

d/da beta(a, b)   = B(a, b) * ( psi(a) - psi(a + b) )

b is a constant double and carries no gradient. Where a gamma factor sits on a pole the sensitivity is NaN.

Examples¶

Example 1. B(2, 3) = 1/12; B(3, 3) = 1/30; B(1, 3) = 1/3.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0, 1.0}).beta(3.0)
) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0833, 0.0333, 0.3333]

Example 2. The beta function is symmetric in its arguments.

pluss::series::print(std::cout,
                     pluss::make_series({2.5}).beta(4.0)) << "\n";
pluss::series::print(std::cout,
                     pluss::make_series({4.0}).beta(2.5)) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0277]
Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0277]

Example 3. The backward pass carries the B(a, b) factor.

auto a = pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
a.beta(3.0).sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.0903, -0.0103]

B(2, 3) * (psi(2) - psi(5)) = (1/12) * (-1.0833) = -0.0903.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Reach for betaln() when accumulating log probabilities. beta() can underflow for large positive arguments where betaln() is still finite.

  • b is a constant and carries no gradient; only a does.

  • Non-positive integer values of a, b, or a + b land on gamma poles and propagate inf / NaN.

Summary¶

beta(b) is B(a, b) = Gamma(a) Gamma(b) / Gamma(a + b), with a from self:

  • symmetric; B(a, 1) = 1/a

  • prefer betaln() for log-domain calculations because beta() loses range

  • differentiable in a; the backward multiplies the digamma difference by B(a, b)

  • b carries no gradient

See Also¶

  • Series::lgamma: the building block; betaln is a combination of three lgamma calls.

  • Series::digamma: the gradient of betaln.

  • Series::mvlgamma: the matrix-argument generalization of the gamma normalizer.
